headline: Ten Prompts, One Launch Video: AI Comes for Creative Production
lede: A short demo posted by Matt Epstein — a full product launch video assembled from roughly ten text prompts — crystallised the anxiety that has accompanied each new AI capability. The tool is **Replit Animation**, a feature from the cloud coding platform Replit that extends the *vibecoding* paradigm from software into video production, powered by Google's Gemini 3.1 Pro.
body:
Replit built its reputation as a browser-based coding environment that lets developers write and run software without local setup. Replit Animation appears to push that same frictionless promise into motion graphics: a user describes what they want — an intro, a problem statement, a features reel — and the system assembles a produced video. The still captured in Epstein's post shows a structured editor with labeled segments (Intro, Problem, Solution, Features), the familiar skeleton of a startup launch video that once required a motion designer, a script, and days of iteration.

*Vibecoding* — a term coined by AI researcher Andrej Karpathy to describe directing software creation through natural-language intent rather than manual authoring — has been Replit's north star for the past two years in code. Extending the concept to video is logically consistent: if you can describe a web app and receive working code, describing a two-minute explainer and receiving a polished clip is the same bet placed on a different medium. Gemini 3.1 Pro, Google's multimodal model, handles the generation.

The economic implication is blunt. Explainer and launch videos — the workhorses of SaaS marketing — have historically required scriptwriters, animators, and voiceover artists, with budgets ranging from a few thousand dollars to tens of thousands. Tools like Replit Animation do not merely speed that process; they restructure who participates in it. A founder with ten prompts and no production skills now occupies a position that previously required a small agency.

Epstein's "we're sooo cooked" framing is a genre unto itself on X — part genuine alarm, part social performance of awe — but the underlying observation is hard to dismiss. The demo is the argument. What is notable is not that AI can generate video (it has been able to for some time) but that the interface is now a structured editor familiar to anyone who has built a slide deck, and the output is plausibly ready to publish.

concepts.definition: A practice popularised by AI researcher Andrej Karpathy in which a person directs an AI system using plain-language descriptions of intent — 'make a landing page for a meditation app' — rather than writing code or files manually. The human acts as editor and prompter; the AI does the authoring. Replit has been a leading platform for this workflow in software development.

A short produced clip, typically 60–180 seconds, that introduces a product by walking through a problem it solves and its key features. Common in SaaS marketing, usually structured as Intro → Problem → Solution → Features → Call to Action. Historically required professional motion design or video production.

An AI model capable of processing and generating more than one type of data — text, images, audio, video — within a unified system. Google's Gemini family is multimodal; applying it to video generation means the model can reason about visuals and motion, not just language.

fact_check: The prompt count in Epstein's own posts is inconsistent: the bookmarked tweet says 10 prompts, but related posts from the same account cite 12 and 18 prompts — suggesting he made multiple attempts or updated his framing across posts. The core claim (a full launch video produced entirely by the tool from a handful of prompts) is consistent across all versions and corroborated by Replit's own announcement text.
